content.title: About
content.content: Ground chicken is finely minced chicken meat, usually without skin or bones. It has a mild flavor, light pink color, and a soft texture, making it a versatile ingredient for many dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ground chicken is often used in recipes that require quick cooking and even flavor distribution.
Compared to beef mince, chicken contains less saturated fat and fewer calories.
Fillet‑only ground chicken is considered a leaner option than mince made from thigh meat.
Ground chicken readily absorbs herbs, spices, and sauces, allowing for a wide range of flavor profiles.
In some countries, pre‑seasoned ground chicken is sold in ready‑to‑cook portions.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Ground chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: When made from chicken breast, the fat content is minimal, suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains vitamins B3, B6 and B12, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Ground chicken supplies iron, zinc and phosphorus.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The high protein level helps keep you feeling full for longer.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Fresh meat can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; proper refrigeration and cooking temperatures are essential.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken.

items.title: Antibiotic residues
items.content: In some regions, chicken may contain trace antibiotics; choose products with appropriate certifications.

items.title: High sodium in seasoned mixes
items.content: Pre‑flavored ground chicken often contains added salt; check the label if you watch sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ground chicken works well for patties, meatballs, sauces, fillings for pies, spring rolls, and Asian stir‑fries. It can be quickly sautéed, boiled, or baked. Before cooking, rinse the meat briefly in cold water and pat dry.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep ground chicken in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for 1‑2 days. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag at ‑18 °C for up to 3 months. Thaw completely in the fridge before use.

chicken-thigh-grilled-without-sauce-skin.title: Chicken thigh, grilled without sauce, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken thigh is the dark meat from the upper part of a bird's leg. Grilled without sauce and without skin, it retains a tender flavor and high protein content while reducing fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dark chicken meat contains more iron and zinc than white meat.
Grilling creates a distinctive aroma through the Maillard reaction of proteins and sugars.
Removing the skin cuts the calorie count by roughly 30%.
Chicken thighs are a staple in many world cuisines, from barbecue to Asian marinades.
When properly grilled, the meat stays juicy thanks to intramuscular fat.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken thigh provides about 25 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies vitamin B6 and niacin, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: The meat contains iron, zinc, and phosphorus, which aid immunity and bone health.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Virtually no carbs make it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Reduced fat when skin is removed
items.content: Skipping the skin lowers saturated fat intake, benefiting cardiovascular health.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Chicken must be cooked to an internal temperature of 74 °C to eliminate salmonella.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium from marinades
items.content: If the meat is marinated, consider the added sodium content.

items.title: Potential carcinogen formation
items.content: Heavy charring can produce heterocyclic amines; grill on moderate heat to limit this.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Skinless grilled thighs can be served as a main dish, sliced into salads, added to wraps, or mixed with vegetables. Light seasoning with salt, pepper, and herbs is optional.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw thighs in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Cooked meat keeps in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days or can be frozen for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Quince (Cydonia oblonga) is a fragrant, golden-yellow fruit related to apples and pears, native to the Caucasus and Iran region. It is very hard, tart, and astringent when raw, and becomes tender, sweet, and pink-orange when cooked. Quince is used in jams, jellies, pastes, compotes, stews, and baked dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Quince is related to apples and pears but is rarely eaten raw because of its hard, astringent flesh.
It has a strong, floral fragrance, and a ripe quince can scent a whole room.
The word marmalade comes from marmelo, the Portuguese word for quince.
Quince is very high in pectin, which is why it sets jams and jellies well.
Quince is used in both sweet and savory dishes, such as stews with meat in Middle Eastern and Central Asian cooking.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Quince is a good source of fiber, including pectin, which supports digestion.

items.title: Provides vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Contains polyphenols
items.content: Quince contains polyphenols with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Quince is relatively low in calories.

items.title: Astringency when raw
items.content: Raw quince is hard and astringent because of tannins and may cause stomach upset or constipation in large amounts. It is best cooked.

items.title: Seeds
items.content: Quince seeds contain compounds that can release cyanide when crushed, so remove and discard them.

items.title: Iron absorption
items.content: Tannins may reduce the absorption of iron from other foods eaten at the same time.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Quince allergy is uncommon but can occur. Rub off the fuzz on the skin before use.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Quince is usually peeled, cored, and cooked by baking, poaching, stewing, or simmering into jams, jellies, and pastes such as membrillo. It can be added to meat stews, pilafs, and baked goods. Cooking turns the flesh tender, sweet, and pink or red.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store quince at room temperature for a few weeks to enjoy its fragrance, or in the refrigerator for a couple of months. Keep it separate from other fruit, since its strong aroma can transfer. Cooked quince should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within about a week.

content.title: About
content.content: Water, enhanced, regular is a purified drinking water enriched with minerals (calcium, magnesium, potassium) and a small amount of electrolytes to support the body’s fluid‑electrolyte balance. It is intended for daily consumption and is suitable for all age groups.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Enhanced water often undergoes additional activated‑carbon filtration to remove residual impurities.
Mineralization helps replenish electrolytes lost during physical activity.
Electrolyte‑enriched water can taste better than plain water for many people.
In some countries these drinks are classified as “mineral water” and must meet specific quality standards.
Packaging in recyclable PET reduces the product’s environmental footprint.

items.title: Improved hydration
items.content: Added minerals aid more efficient water retention in the body, especially during intense exercise.

items.title: Electrolyte balance
items.content: Potassium and magnesium support muscle function and nerve signaling, reducing the risk of cramps.

items.title: Bone support
items.content: Calcium contributes to maintaining bone density when consumed regularly.

items.title: Neutral pH
items.content: A pH around 7.0 helps maintain the body’s acid‑base balance.

items.title: No added sugar
items.content: The product contains no added sugars, making it suitable for low‑glycemic diets.

items.title: Excess mineral intake
items.content: Overconsumption may lead to elevated calcium or magnesium levels, which can be problematic for certain medical conditions.

items.title: Allergy to additives
items.content: Rarely, individuals may be sensitive to specific mineral additives used in the formulation.

items.title: Not a medical replacement
items.content: Severe dehydration or electrolyte disorders require specialized medical treatment, not just enhanced water.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink regularly throughout the day, especially before, during, and after exercise. It can also be used as a base for diluting fruit juices or sports drinks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, reseal the bottle and consume within 3–5 days.
